chapters: Nice, silly and the long road

units.t: Words That Flipped Their Meaning.
Part one. Nice, silly and the long road.
Imagine being called nice in the year 1300.
You might not have been flattered.
In this lesson, we'll look at words that have changed their meanings, sometimes completely, over the centuries.
We'll see the main ways words drift, and why it happens at all.
Let's begin with the word in that opening line.
Nice.
N, I, C, E.
Here's an everyday example of how we use it now.
It was really nice of the neighbours to bring the bins in while we were away.
Nice came into English from French in the late 1200s.
It goes back to the Latin word nescius, which means not knowing, or ignorant.
And that's exactly what it first meant in English.
A nice person was foolish, ignorant or silly.
From there, the word went on a remarkable journey.
Over the next few centuries, nice came to mean timid, then fussy and fastidious, then dainty and delicate.
By the 1500s, it could mean precise and careful.
You can still hear that meaning today in the phrase a nice distinction, which means a fine or subtle one.
Only in the 1700s did nice start to mean pleasant or agreeable.
The kind and thoughtful sense came even later, in the 1800s.
So in about five hundred years, nice went from foolish to kind, taking several detours along the way.
Our second word made almost the opposite journey.
Silly.
S, I, L, L, Y.
For example, don't be silly, you're not going to wear thongs to a job interview.
In Old English, the ancestor of silly meant happy, lucky or blessed.
It's related to the modern German word selig, which still means blessed.
Around 1200, silly came to mean innocent.
From innocent, it slid to pitiable, deserving sympathy.
Then to weak.
Then, by the late 1500s, to feeble-minded and foolish, which is roughly where we are today.
You can see the logic at each step.
Someone who is innocent may be easily fooled.
Someone who is easily fooled may seem simple.
And someone who seems simple may be called foolish.
Each small step made sense, but after a few centuries, the word had travelled from blessed to brainless.
Here's the key point.
Words rarely jump straight from one meaning to its opposite.
They drift, one small step at a time, usually over generations.
Each generation only notices a slight shift, if they notice anything at all.
It's only when you line the steps up across centuries that the change looks dramatic.
Linguists have names for the main directions words drift in.
When a word's meaning gets more negative, like silly, it's called pejoration.
That comes from the Latin word for worse.
When a word's meaning gets more positive, like nice, it's called amelioration, from the Latin for better.
We'll meet both of these many times in the next part.
Part two. Worse and better.
Let's start with a pair that everyone mentions when they talk about changing words.
Awful.
A, W, F, U, L.
For example, the traffic on the freeway was awful this morning.
Awful was originally just what it looks like, full of awe.
Around 1300, it meant something that inspired awe, wonder or dread.
The presence of God was awful.
A great storm at sea was awful.
It was a serious, powerful word.
But in the early 1800s, people started using it to mean simply very bad.
By then, the sense of awe had drained away.
Today, awful describes a traffic jam, a cold cup of tea or a bad joke.
Its modern replacement is awesome, which took over the job of expressing awe.
And of course, awesome itself is now going the same way.
When someone calls a sausage roll awesome, nobody's standing in wonder before the Almighty.
Our next word went the other way.
Terrific.
T, E, R, R, I, F, I, C.
For example, you did a terrific job on that presentation.
Terrific was first used in English in the 1660s, by the poet John Milton.
It meant terrifying, causing terror.
By the early 1800s, it had weakened to mean very great or severe, as in a terrific storm or a terrific headache.
Then, in the late 1800s, it flipped to mean excellent.
So awful and terrific both started out frightening.
One ended up bad, and one ended up good.
Our next word is a lovely example of a word that changed sides.
Egregious.
E, G, R, E, G, I, O, U, S.
For example, charging $12 for a small bottle of water at the airport is an egregious rip-off.
Egregious comes from Latin, meaning rising out of the flock, or standing out from the herd.
When it came into English in the 1500s, it meant distinguished and excellent.
An egregious scholar was an outstanding one.
But within a few decades, people started using it ironically.
Calling a fool an egregious fool was a sarcastic kind of praise.
The irony stuck, and the negative sense slowly took over.
Now egregious means outstandingly bad, and almost nobody remembers it was once a compliment.
Here's one more worsening word, with a sweet start.
Bully.
B, U, L, L, Y.
For example, the school has a clear plan for dealing with any child who's being a bully.
In the 1500s, bully was a term of affection.
It meant sweetheart or darling, and it could be used for a man or a woman.
It probably came from a Dutch word for lover or brother.
In Shakespeare's Henry the Fifth, a character called Pistol declares his affection for the king with the words, I love the lovely bully.
Over the next century or so, bully slid from darling, to fine fellow, to a blustering show-off.
By the late 1600s, it meant someone who picks on the weak.
A trace of the old meaning survives in the phrase bully for you, which means good for you, though today it's usually said sarcastically.
Part three. Broader, narrower and literally.
Words don't only get better or worse.
Sometimes their meanings get wider or narrower.
Linguists call these broadening and narrowing.
Let's start with narrowing.
Deer.
D, E, E, R.
For example, we slowed right down because a deer was standing by the side of the road.
In Old English, the ancestor of deer simply meant animal, any wild animal at all.
German still has a close cousin, Tier, which means animal.
You can hear the old meaning in Shakespeare's King Lear.
A character describes living on mice and rats, and such small deer.
He doesn't mean tiny antlered animals.
He means small creatures in general.
Over time, deer narrowed to mean one particular kind of animal, and the word animal, borrowed from Latin, took over the general job.
Meat followed a similar path.
In Old English, meat meant food of any kind.
That's why we still have the word sweetmeat, for a sweet treat, and the old saying one man's meat is another man's poison.
Our next word narrowed too, in a way that surprises most people.
Girl.
G, I, R, L.
For example, the girl at the front desk was incredibly helpful.
When girl first appeared in Middle English, around 1300, it meant a child or young person of either sex.
In Chaucer's Canterbury Tales, written in the late 1300s, the phrase the young girls of the diocese means the young people of the district, boys and girls alike.
Only later did girl narrow to mean a young female.
Interestingly, it has stretched a little again since then, because today it's often used for women of any age, as in a girls' night out.
Now for broadening, where a meaning gets wider.
Holiday.
H, O, L, I, D, A, Y.
For example, we're taking the kids up the coast for the school holidays.
You can probably hear where this one came from.
A holiday was originally a holy day, a religious festival.
Because people didn't work on holy days, the word gradually came to mean any day off.
Then it broadened again, to mean a whole trip away.
Today, a holiday can involve a caravan park, a theme park or a week on the couch, with nothing holy about it at all.
Dog is another broadening word, though its early history is a little murky.
In Old English, the usual word for a dog was hound.
The rare word docga seems to have been used for one particular kind of powerful dog.
Over time, dog spread to cover every breed, from a Great Dane to a chihuahua.
Hound went the opposite way and narrowed, and now it usually means a hunting dog.
So the two words swapped places.
Our final word is the one people argue about most.
Literally.
L, I, T, E, R, A, L, L, Y.
For example, I was so tired I literally fell asleep standing up on the train.
Literally originally meant exactly, word for word, not as a metaphor.
But people have been using it as an intensifier, simply to add emphasis, for a surprisingly long time.
One well-known early example comes from 1769, in a novel by the writer Frances Brooke.
A character says that a lucky man, surrounded by fine women, is literally feeding among the lilies.
He isn't, of course, actually grazing in a garden.
Much-loved writers like Charles Dickens and Mark Twain used it the same way.
When someone says their head literally exploded, they're following a path that very has already travelled.
Very comes from an old French word meaning true.
It used to mean truly or really, and you can still hear that in old phrases like the very thing, meaning exactly the thing.
Over time, very became a simple intensifier, and nobody minds at all.
Major dictionaries in Australia, Britain and the United States now record the emphatic sense of literally, usually with a note that some people dislike it.
That's what dictionaries do.
They describe how people actually use words, rather than dictating how they should.
So why do words drift at all?
There are a few main reasons.
One is that strong words wear out.
If you use awful or terrific for everything, they lose their punch, so we reach for new ones.
Another is irony and sarcasm, which is how egregious flipped.
Say something ironically often enough, and the ironic meaning can become the real one.
A third is politeness.
When a word for something uncomfortable starts to sound harsh, people swap in a gentler one.
Over time, the new word picks up the same negative feeling, and it gets replaced too.
The psychologist Steven Pinker called this the euphemism treadmill.
Words for the toilet are a classic example.
Toilet itself was once a polite word, borrowed from French, for a small cloth used while dressing and doing your hair.
It moved to the dressing room, then to the room with the plumbing, and eventually it started to sound a bit blunt.
So people reached for bathroom, washroom, restroom and powder room, and Australians, of course, reached for the loo and the dunny.
And finally, the world itself changes, and words stretch or shrink to fit it.
Knowing all this can make you a bit more relaxed about language change.
It can also make old writing easier to understand.
When a character in an old novel is called nice, or a hymn describes something as awful, it's worth pausing to ask what the word meant back then.
Very often, it meant something quite different from what we'd assume today.
The words you grew up with once meant something else, and the words that annoy you now may be perfectly normal in fifty years.
To sum up, words drift one small step at a time, getting better or worse, wider or narrower.
Nice once meant foolish, silly once meant blessed, and awful once meant full of awe.
Language change isn't decay, it's simply what living languages do.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What did nice mean when it first came into English in the 1200s?
Answer. Foolish or ignorant.
Question two. What's the name for a word's meaning getting worse over time, as happened to silly and bully?
Answer. Pejoration.
Question three. Deer once meant any animal. Is that an example of broadening or narrowing?
Answer. Narrowing. The meaning shrank to one kind of animal.
That's the end of Words That Flipped Their Meaning. Terrific work, in every sense. See you next time.
